title: Michael Robartes and the Dancer
author: W. B. Yeats
note: Easter 1916 pressure in a tight 1921 book — occult, desire, and society.

breaths.text: MICHAEL ROBARTES AND THE DANCER
He: Opinion is not worth a rush;
He: In this altar-piece the knight,
He: Who grips his long spear so to push
He: That dragon through the fading light,
He: Loved the lady; and it’s plain
He: The half-dead dragon was her thought,
He: That every morning rose again
He: And dug its claws and shrieked and fought.
He: Could the impossible come to pass
He: She would have time to turn her eyes,
He: Her lover thought, upon the glass
He: And on the instant would grow wise.
She: You mean they argued.
He: Put it so;
He: But bear in mind your lover’s wage
He: Is what your looking-glass can show,
He: And that he will turn green with rage
He: At all that is not pictured there.
She: May I not put myself to college?
He: Go pluck Athena by the hair;
He: For what mere book can grant a knowledge
He: With an impassioned gravity
He: Appropriate to that beating breast,
He: That vigorous thigh, that dreaming eye?
He: And may the devil take the rest.
She: And must no beautiful woman be
She: Learned like a man?
He: Paul Veronese
And all his sacred company
Imagined bodies all their days
By the lagoon you love so much,
For proud, soft, ceremonious proof
That all must come to sight and touch;
While Michael Angelo’s Sistine roof
His ‘Morning’ and his ‘Night’ disclose
How sinew that has been pulled tight,
Or it may be loosened in repose,
Can rule by supernatural right
Yet be but sinew.
She: I have heard said
She: There is great danger in the body.
He: Did God in portioning wine and bread
He: Give man His thought or His mere body?
She: My wretched dragon is perplexed.
He: I have principles to prove me right.
He: It follows from this Latin text
He: That blest souls are not composite.
He: And that all beautiful women may
He: Live in uncomposite blessedness,
He: And lead us to the like--if they
He: Will banish every thought, unless
He: The lineaments that please their view
He: When the long looking-glass is full,
He: Even from the foot-sole think it too.
She: They say such different things at school.
She: SOLOMON AND THE WITCH
She: And thus declared that Arab lady:
She: “Last night, where under the wild moon
She: On grassy mattress I had laid me,
Within my arms great Solomon,
I suddenly cried out in a strange tongue
Not his, not mine.”
And he that knew
All sounds by bird or angel sung
Answered: “A crested cockerel crew
Upon a blossoming apple bough
Three hundred years before the Fall,
And never crew again till now,
And would not now but that he thought,
Chance being at one with Choice at last.
All that the brigand apple brought
And this foul world were dead at last.
He that crowed out eternity
Thought to have crowed it in again.
A lover with a spider’s eye
Will find out some appropriate pain,
Aye, though all passion’s in the glance,
For every nerve: lover tests lover
With cruelties of Choice and Chance;
And when at last that murder’s over
Maybe the bride-bed brings despair
For each an imagined image brings
And finds a real image there;
Yet the world ends when these two things,
Though several, are a single light,
When oil and wick are burned in one;
Therefore a blessed moon last night
Gave Sheba to her Solomon.”
“Yet the world stays:”
“If that be so,
Your cockerel found us in the wrong
Although he thought it worth a crow.
Maybe an image is too strong
Or maybe is not strong enough.”
“The night has fallen; not a sound
